sections.heading: Visualization and graphics
paragraphs: Visualization turns information into imagery, graphs, or animation, making large or time-varying information easier to understand. In modeling and simulation it includes data analysis and visual training simulations; computer graphics is its core technology. Computer graphics generates or manipulates images using software and hardware.

sections.heading: Graphics hardware and 3D geometry
paragraphs: Realistic graphics requires computation and memory. The slides trace dedicated workstation acceleration in the mid-1980s, 2D PC acceleration in the mid-1990s, 3D PC acceleration in the late 1990s, and programmable vertex and pixel shaders in the early 2000s. Convex polygon meshes simplify rendering: a line segment joining any two points in a convex object lies entirely within it.

sections.heading: Coordinates and transformations
paragraphs: A point represents a location without size or shape; a vector has direction and length but no location. Graphics use Cartesian components, matrices, and homogeneous coordinates to express transformations. Affine transformations preserve collinearity and ratios of distances along a line; translation, rotation, and scaling are examples. They can represent changes in dynamic objects.

sections.heading: Synthetic cameras and projection
paragraphs: A synthetic camera maps 3D objects to a 2D projection using camera parameters. Location, target location, and up direction position and orient it; world coordinates are converted into camera coordinates. Perspective projection uses a finite center of projection and rays through object points. Parallel projection uses a direction of projection and six clipping planes; orthographic projection has a direction perpendicular to the projection plane and preserves distances and directions along that plane, useful for CAD measurements.

sections.heading: Lighting, shading, and textures
paragraphs: Rods primarily support low-light vision, while cones support color vision. Ambient light gives uniform illumination independent of location and direction. A point light radiates equally in all directions and attenuates with distance. A spotlight is specified by location, direction, and cutoff angle; a directional light models a distant source such as sunlight. Reflection describes light–object interaction, shading determines colors within polygons, and texture mapping enriches appearance without greatly increasing geometric complexity.

sections.heading: Graphics software
paragraphs: The slides identify OpenGL as a cross-platform low-level graphics API and Direct3D as a Microsoft 3D graphics API; they also describe OpenSceneGraph as an open-source cross-platform library, MATLAB for numerical work and visualization, and Maya for 3D modeling and animation. These slides describe historical tools and should not be treated as an up-to-date product survey. Page 57 calls Java 3D a programming language; more accurately, Java 3D is an API for 3D graphics, not the Java language itself.

sections.heading: VV&A vocabulary and requirements
paragraphs: The simuland is the real object, process, or phenomenon of interest; the referent is the knowledge available about it, both quantitative and qualitative. A conceptual model documents represented and omitted aspects and assumptions, serving as a specification for an executable model. A simulation executes a model over time and produces results. Requirements, driven by intended use, specify what must be modeled and how accurately.

sections.heading: Verification, validation, and accreditation
paragraphs: Verification examines transformational accuracy: whether requirements, conceptual model, and executable implementation are consistent. Validation examines representational accuracy: how accurately the model and its results represent the simuland, including the range of credible inputs. Accreditation is a responsible authority’s official decision that a model is acceptable for a specific purpose, informed by V&V results. Neither general apparent realism nor verification alone establishes validity for every use.

sections.heading: Project types and credibility
paragraphs: A simulation study primarily seeks insight; code need not be its primary deliverable. Simulation software development delivers executable software expected to be reused and maintained. A simulation event uses existing models for a particular objective, with scenario, data, logistics, and security potentially important. Credibility concerns whether results are considered acceptable for an application and costs resources to develop; managers balance credibility requirements against available resources.

sections.heading: Errors and bounds of validity
paragraphs: Type I error is not using a valid model, with likelihood called model builder’s risk. Type II is using an invalid model, with likelihood called model user’s risk. Type III is using a model valid for another purpose but inappropriate for the intended application, with likelihood called model accreditor’s risk. The gravity examples illustrate bounds of validity: a simple approximation can be adequate only over a limited range, while the gravity model depends on assumptions including negligible air resistance and proximity to Earth’s surface.

sections.heading: Informal and static methods
paragraphs: Informal V&V relies on qualitative expert judgment. Inspection compares artifacts such as code against design equations; face validation compares observed results against experts’ knowledge of the simuland. The Turing test is a specialized face-validation approach for human behavior. Static methods examine characteristics without executing a simulation: data analysis checks definitions, operations, dependencies, and flows, while cause–effect graphing compares important causal relationships between simuland and conceptual model.

sections.heading: Dynamic and formal methods
paragraphs: Dynamic V&V executes models and evaluates results. Sensitivity analysis compares the magnitude and variability of outputs and can reveal influential inputs; predictive validation compares specific corresponding outcomes; comparison testing runs multiple models with the same input. Regression and hypothesis testing provide statistical approaches. Formal methods use mathematical proof: inductive assertions address executable-model correctness along execution paths, and predicate calculus can express and compare simuland and conceptual-model properties. Appropriate methods depend on the model, available data, and practical execution, and multiple methods are often combined.

cards.question: Why use visualization in simulation?
options: To convey large or time-varying information visually
To eliminate all model assumptions
To replace every numerical output with audio
To prove a model valid automatically
cards.correct_answer: To convey large or time-varying information visually

cards.question: What is a convex object?
options: One with no straight edges
One whose points all lie on one plane
One that must be a sphere
One in which every segment joining two of its points lies entirely inside it
cards.correct_answer: One in which every segment joining two of its points lies entirely inside it

cards.question: Which describes a mathematical vector in the slides?
options: It has size and shape but no direction
It is necessarily a point on a surface
It has length and direction but no location
It has location but neither length nor direction
cards.correct_answer: It has length and direction but no location

cards.question: What is the role of homogeneous coordinates in 3D graphics?
options: They convert every 3D object directly into audio
They allow affine transformations such as translation and rotation to be expressed by matrix multiplication
They eliminate the need for camera coordinates
They guarantee all rendered objects are convex
cards.correct_answer: They allow affine transformations such as translation and rotation to be expressed by matrix multiplication

cards.question: Which transformation family includes translation, rotation, and scaling?
options: Affine transformations
Hypothesis tests
Texture compression
Accreditation decisions
cards.correct_answer: Affine transformations

cards.question: What does a synthetic camera produce from a 3D scene and camera parameters?
options: A new physical camera
A proof of model validity
A simulation requirement
A 2D projected image
cards.correct_answer: A 2D projected image

cards.question: Which three parameters position and orient the slide’s camera?
options: Simulation time, event count, and queue length
Near plane, model credibility, and screen resolution
Camera location, target location, and up direction
Light color, surface texture, and pixel depth
cards.correct_answer: Camera location, target location, and up direction

cards.question: What characterizes perspective projection?
options: It cannot produce a 2D image
Projectors run from a finite center of projection through object points
All projectors have a single parallel direction with no finite center
The direction of projection is necessarily perpendicular to the image plane
cards.correct_answer: Projectors run from a finite center of projection through object points

cards.question: How is parallel projection specified in the slides?
options: By a direction of projection and six clipping planes
By a finite center of projection alone
By point-light color and intensity
By validation and accreditation criteria
cards.correct_answer: By a direction of projection and six clipping planes

cards.question: When is a parallel projection orthographic?
options: When every object is infinitely far from the camera
When the projection plane is curved
When the model uses only perspective projectors
When the direction of projection is perpendicular to the projection plane
cards.correct_answer: When the direction of projection is perpendicular to the projection plane

cards.question: Why are orthographic projections useful in architectural design and CAD?
options: They automatically validate architectural safety
They require no geometric model
They preserve distances and directions along the projection plane for measurement
They make every distant object appear larger
cards.correct_answer: They preserve distances and directions along the projection plane for measurement

cards.question: Which photoreceptors mainly support low-intensity vision?
options: Pixels
Rods
Cones
Camera projectors
cards.correct_answer: Rods

cards.question: Which light model illuminates all objects uniformly regardless of location and direction?
options: Ambient light
Spotlight
Point light with distance attenuation
A finite perspective camera
cards.correct_answer: Ambient light

cards.question: What distinguishes the ideal point light in the slides?
options: It illuminates only outside a cone
It has no location and is always at infinity
It illuminates uniformly regardless of distance
It emits equally in every direction and attenuates with distance
cards.correct_answer: It emits equally in every direction and attenuates with distance

cards.question: Which parameters define a spotlight?
options: Six clipping planes alone
Only color and an image file
Location, direction, and cutoff angle
Location, target, and camera up vector
cards.correct_answer: Location, direction, and cutoff angle

cards.question: Which source is appropriately approximated by a directional light?
options: A uniform ambient field with no direction
Sunlight from a very distant source
A nearby light bulb whose distance attenuation matters
A cone-shaped flashlight with a cutoff angle
cards.correct_answer: Sunlight from a very distant source

cards.question: What is the main benefit of texture mapping described in the slides?
options: Richer visual appearance without greatly increasing geometric complexity
Proof that the model is accurate
Elimination of all light sources
Conversion of a conceptual model into requirements
cards.correct_answer: Richer visual appearance without greatly increasing geometric complexity

cards.question: Which graphics API is described as cross-platform?
options: Direct3D only on Xbox and Windows
The accreditation process
The Turing test
OpenGL
cards.correct_answer: OpenGL

cards.question: In an assembly-line simulation, what is the simuland?
options: The authority granting accreditation
The model’s randomly generated output only
The automobile assembly process being represented
The model’s source code only
cards.correct_answer: The automobile assembly process being represented

cards.question: What is the referent?
options: The actual object independent of what is known about it
The developers’ body of knowledge about the simuland
The final accreditation certificate
Only the compiled executable model
cards.correct_answer: The developers’ body of knowledge about the simuland

cards.question: What does a conceptual model document?
options: Represented and omitted simuland aspects and model assumptions
Only the final simulation results
Only the source code’s syntax
The authority’s accreditation decision alone
cards.correct_answer: Represented and omitted simuland aspects and model assumptions

cards.question: What is an executable model?
options: A description that can never be executed
The physical simuland itself
An accreditation authority
An implementation that can be executed to simulate the simuland as specified conceptually
cards.correct_answer: An implementation that can be executed to simulate the simuland as specified conceptually

cards.question: What determines which simuland aspects and accuracy levels requirements specify?
options: The graphics API vendor
Whether the model is open source
The intended application
The number of animation frames alone
cards.correct_answer: The intended application

cards.question: Which question is principally a verification question?
options: Is a pilot familiar with the simulator controls?
Does the executable code correctly implement the conceptual model?
Does simulated behavior accurately represent the simuland?
Has an authority officially approved this use?
cards.correct_answer: Does the executable code correctly implement the conceptual model?

cards.question: Which question is principally a validation question?
options: How close are model results to the simuland’s behavior?
Does source code implement its conceptual specification?
Is the executable delivered in the required format?
Has the responsible authority issued certification?
cards.correct_answer: How close are model results to the simuland’s behavior?

cards.question: What is accreditation?
options: Proof that any use of a model is valid
An automatic consequence of compiling code
The process of drawing a conceptual model
Official certification by a responsible authority that a model is acceptable for a specific purpose
cards.correct_answer: Official certification by a responsible authority that a model is acceptable for a specific purpose

cards.question: What is the primary deliverable of a simulation software development project?
options: An existing model’s one-time scenario only
A physical prototype of the simuland
An executable model expected to be reused and maintained
Insight alone, with code never a primary deliverable
cards.correct_answer: An executable model expected to be reused and maintained

cards.question: What is a simulation event?
options: A synonym for the real-world simuland
A particular use of existing model or models for a specific objective
A project whose only objective is creating reusable simulation software
An automatic formal proof
cards.correct_answer: A particular use of existing model or models for a specific objective

cards.question: A valid flight simulator is not used because the authority is not persuaded to certify it. Which error is this?
options: Type I error, associated with model builder’s risk
Type II error, associated with model user’s risk
Type III error, associated with model accreditor’s risk
A correct accreditation decision by definition
cards.correct_answer: Type I error, associated with model builder’s risk

cards.question: An invalid flight simulator is used to train pilots. Which error is this?
options: Type I error, associated with model builder’s risk
Type III error, associated only with model accreditor’s risk
A harmless visualization issue by definition
Type II error, associated with model user’s risk
cards.correct_answer: Type II error, associated with model user’s risk

cards.question: A simulator valid for one aircraft type is used to qualify pilots for a different type. Which error is illustrated?
options: Type II: never executing the model
No error because any valid model is valid for every purpose
Type III: using a model inappropriate for its intended application
Type I: refusing to use a valid model
cards.correct_answer: Type III: using a model inappropriate for its intended application

cards.question: What is the purpose of establishing bounds of validity?
options: Guarantee accreditation for all future applications
Identify conditions under which a model can be sufficiently accurate and reduce validation risk
Prove the model works for every possible input
Eliminate the need for intended-use requirements
cards.correct_answer: Identify conditions under which a model can be sufficiently accurate and reduce validation risk

cards.question: What does face validation compare?
options: Simulation results with knowledgeable observers’ expectations of simuland behavior
Program code with its design specification only
An accreditation certificate with a budget
Two programming languages without executing a simulation
cards.correct_answer: Simulation results with knowledgeable observers’ expectations of simuland behavior

cards.question: What is inspection in the slides?
options: A validation method requiring independent physical experiments in every case
An official certification for any use
A method that requires no human assessment
A verification method comparing artifacts such as code and conceptual design
cards.correct_answer: A verification method comparing artifacts such as code and conceptual design

cards.question: What distinguishes static V&V from dynamic V&V?
options: Dynamic methods cannot compare numeric results
Static methods are identical to accreditation
Static methods assess characteristics without executing a simulation; dynamic methods execute the model
Static methods always use real-time animation
cards.correct_answer: Static methods assess characteristics without executing a simulation; dynamic methods execute the model

cards.question: What does data analysis check in static verification?
options: Whether the simuland is a physical object
Data definitions and operations in the executable model against the conceptual model
Only whether the simulation looks realistic
Whether an authority issued an accreditation certificate
cards.correct_answer: Data definitions and operations in the executable model against the conceptual model

cards.question: What does cause–effect graphing validate?
options: Important cause-and-effect relationships in the simuland against those in the conceptual model
The choice of graphics card against the budget
The accreditation signature against a software license
Only the formatting of simulation output
cards.correct_answer: Important cause-and-effect relationships in the simuland against those in the conceptual model

cards.question: What can sensitivity analysis reveal?
options: Whether an executable exists without examining it
The name of the accrediting authority
That every output is correct for every input
Which input variations have the greatest impact on model results
cards.correct_answer: Which input variations have the greatest impact on model results

cards.question: How does comparison testing use multiple models?
options: Compare only their source file names
Accredit each model without execution
Run them with the same inputs and compare their results
Use unrelated inputs and assume differences prove validity
cards.correct_answer: Run them with the same inputs and compare their results

cards.question: How is hypothesis testing applied to model validation in the slides?
options: Compare the size of two executable files
Treat multiple simulation results as a sample and compare their distribution with a valid-results distribution
Prove all source code correct by inspecting one screenshot
Replace the simuland with a different application
cards.correct_answer: Treat multiple simulation results as a sample and compare their distribution with a valid-results distribution

cards.question: What is the core idea of inductive assertions?
options: Prove that beginning assertions and execution-path instructions imply ending assertions
Ask experts whether an animation looks plausible
Compare unrelated model outputs without running them
Officially certify all future applications
cards.correct_answer: Prove that beginning assertions and execution-path instructions imply ending assertions

cards.question: Why might a project combine multiple V&V methods?
options: Every method is mandatory for every model
One method always proves suitability for all applications
The model’s intended use is irrelevant
Different methods address different verification and validation concerns, subject to model and data constraints
cards.correct_answer: Different methods address different verification and validation concerns, subject to model and data constraints
